lines.dialogue: An hour before dusk at the Grammar Mill. The week's last pages lie on the cooling tray, and the bell for the ferryman's mother will ring at dusk.
lines.stage_directions: Pricha - Lek to the whole landing - sets a tin lamp on the Type Floor. Trays of metal type sit under their dust; the hand press is folded for the night.

lines.dialogue: I brought the lamp, Pom. Four rows are cool enough to copy. Let's finish before the bell.
Then we copy only what is cool. The school can wait one morning for the rest.
Twelve hours on the tray, clerk. A page pulled early casts crooked and lies forever.
The ferryman's mother goes under the earth at dusk, and the temple expects its clerks. I keep the tray; I do not keep the bell.
It is a strange place to stand - a page on one side, a funeral on the other.
The mill cools everything on a schedule - pages, rice, grief. A thing that is cooling only looks still. Underneath it is still hot enough to burn you.
Then what do I do with it while it cools?
No one goes further than the tray today. Whatever is left after dark belongs to whoever is buried.
Four rows and one bell, Lek. I can read alone, but two voices carry a page faster than one.
I lock the tray at the lamp, whatever the lamp thinks. Pages do not pour merit, and water does not copy pages.
Then hold the lamp steady, and we will see which of us finishes first.

line.dialogue: The lamp burns till dark and the bell rings at dusk, young clerk. I hold the tray. Which of the two holds you?

choices.description: I will stay and copy the four rows, and let the bell ring without me.

line.dialogue: I see Pom slide my copy to the tray's corner and touch the glass twice, the way the monitor blesses a cool page.
I see Pom take the pen from my hand and copy the last row himself, slower, while the bell dies over the water.

choices.description: I will go to the temple at dusk and pour for the ferryman's mother, and let the tray lock with a row uncopied.

line.dialogue: I hear Pom come in behind me at the bell and stand at my shoulder without a word.
I see the tray locked when we return, and Pom reading the last warm row through the glass by lamplight.

choices.description: I will ask the monitor to let the north window keep the last page overnight - ledge air is cool air - and go pour with a clear head.

line.dialogue: I see the monitor lift the window latch herself, as if the ledge had always been a tray.
I see the monitor shake her head at the window and lock the tray on the hour, uncopied page and all.

lines.dialogue: The next morning at the Rice Ledger; the open book under its glass, the red block shaped like a grain silo, and a widow keeping her ten minutes on the Cooling Bench.
lines.stage_directions: Pom lays out his rice-paper slips. The water-clock runs.

lines.dialogue: Clerk, my friend copies entries for the school, and your bench runs on water-time. Give us the ten minutes and we will not breathe on your case.
The bench cools what the glass cannot. Sit. The widow had her say at the Stamp Table; the record will have its own.
Then I will copy the say and the record both, side by side, and keep them honest.
We record weight, not will. Her say came warm. The record is cooled to 'yield reduced by natural variance.' That is the whole of it.
A man I shared a school bench with wrote appeals like hers. The papers came back cooled the same way. He was the better graduate, and he is two provinces from any window now.
lines.stage_directions: Pom's pen stops over the slip. He does not look up when he says it.

lines.dialogue: The appeal goes up the river on the evening boat.
And it will be read by the same eyes that cooled it.
Probably. So speak plainly if you speak at all.
The record cools what it can, Lek. What it cannot cool, it sends up the river where nobody has to watch it cook.
Pom, your slips carry more grief than the case holds. Set one down before it cools you through.
The glass keeps one pen. I will lend it for your copies, clerk to clerk, but the line under it stands as it stands.

line.dialogue: Her say cools on the bench and my red block is warm in my hand. Speak her measure into my record and it becomes her claim, or hold your tongue and copy what stands. Which clerk are you?

choices.description: I will hold my tongue, copy the cooled line as it stands, and let the widow keep her measure.

line.dialogue: I see Pom initial my copied slip without a correction and set it in the dry row.
I see Pom blot my copied line with his cloth and begin the slip again, slower.

choices.description: I will speak the widow's measure into the record in her own words, and let the red block fall where it falls.

line.dialogue: I hear the widow's measure go into the record in her own words, and Pom's pen does not stop.
I see the clerk's margin take the word 'interrupted' and Pom close his slip halfway.

choices.description: I will ask the clerk to read the appeal aloud once more at the bench, so the cooled line must carry her measure to the last grain.

line.dialogue: I see the clerk read the appeal a second time and the cooled line grow one word longer.
I see the clerk refuse the second reading and stamp the cooled line as it stood.

lines.dialogue: Before sunrise at the Charcoal Hearth; the whole night's heat held under one ash lid, and Pom unfolding a page the tray never saw.
lines.stage_directions: The stoker hums without a tune. The smoke rises in a thin, straight column.

lines.dialogue: Pom, tell me the pit knows we are coming.
The pit knows everything. One page, folded small. Two pages make smoke, and smoke tells.
Sit on the Waiting Stones. The coals were fed at dusk and smothered at dark. They will take your page the way they take a rice cake, slow and all the way through.
lines.stage_directions: She lifts the ash lid. No flame answers; the embers lie below breath-level, banked and red.

lines.dialogue: I can smell grief in the smoke before anyone speaks. Yours is folded small. Sit closer.
I am standing right in front of the pit and I cannot see the page at all.
Full light closes the pit, and the district counts its smoke from the river. When I say closed, I mean it.
Then the bowl pours now, and the page takes its hour from the coals.
So 'closed' means the page stays in, and 'open' means the river sees the smoke. There is no third door.
There is no skin here, Lek. Whatever is still cooking, the smoke will say it for you.
lines.stage_directions: Pom folds the page smaller. On its back, in a younger hand, three words. He closes it before the stoker can see.

lines.dialogue: Wind off the river. The smoke column will stand up straight and tell on us.
Then the coals are faster than the morning. Do not watch my hands, Lek. Hold your bowl.

line.dialogue: The gust is on the water. Hold your bowl over the lid and let the page char, or put the bowl down and take the page back with your hands. The pit does not wait for both.

choices.description: I will hold the bowl steady and let the page char all the way through.

line.dialogue: I see Pom watch the lid through the smoke and nod once, as at a bell rung on time.
I see the gust take the page's corner and Pom's hand close on nothing.

choices.description: I will put the bowl down on the stones, reach in, and take the page back before it is gone.

line.dialogue: I hear Pom take the half-charred page from my fingers and say my name without ice.
I see Pom take the page back with two fingers and lay it in the pit a second time.

choices.description: I will ask the stoker to bank the lid deep and let the pit close at full light with the page still charring. I will pour over the closed lid.

line.dialogue: I see the stoker bank the lid with her own rod, and the smoke lie down.
I see the stoker hold the lid shut against the wind and shake her head at the sky.

lines.dialogue: Dusk on the School Veranda; the bowls in a row for the evening pour, and the tax clerk coming up the steps with his red block.
lines.stage_directions: The pond keeps the same circle it keeps every evening.

lines.dialogue: The school copies ride the evening boat. My book is open and my stamp is warm.
The landing sits down to hear its week first. The district can hold its book one turn of the water.
Clerk, you are standing right here in the circle. Sit with us one turn of the water.
My father pressed thumbprints on the other side of that glass. I will stand, and I will listen, and then I will stamp.
Then hear the phrase the mill cooled this week. It goes back to the landing before it goes down the river - standing order of the floor.
That was the week, as the floor said it.
lines.stage_directions: He reads the week's phrase aloud, once, the way it was spoken on the mill floor. Nobody corrects him. The clerk's thumb finds the block and waits.

lines.dialogue: A phrase that cools a whole night and still sounds warm.
The stamp thinks it is the coolest thing on the landing, but it cools on our bench like anybody's sentence.
On the veranda bench, under the sky's own tray, until dawn. Delay is quarantine; the district's stamp can cool like anybody's sentence.
The boat leaves without it, then. I will write that the stamp was warm and had to cool. My book will not lie.
The week is copied, the page is cool, and the boat can wait for the morning water.

line.dialogue: Young clerk, my stamp cools on your bench and my legs are tired. Do you rise and meet me with the bowl still full, or do I stand here until the water is poured?

choices.description: I will stay over the bowl and finish the pour, and ask the clerk's pardon from where I sit.

line.dialogue: I see Pom set a third stool for the clerk without looking up from the page.
I see the clerk hold his book against his chest and wait out the pour on his feet.

choices.description: I will set the bowl down, rise, and give the clerk the full bow a host owes a guest.

line.dialogue: I hear the clerk answer my bow with the deep one a guest owes a host.
I see the clerk return my bow with the small one for a debtor.

choices.description: I will greet him from where I sit, bowl in hand, and bid him take the third stool for one turn of the water.

line.dialogue: I see the clerk take the stool and the water pass from my bowl to his cup.
I see the clerk stay standing, and the bowl go cool in my hands.
